passage: Rain had flooded the lane outside the cyber café, and the power kept dipping, so the mock-test results took ten minutes to load for Yamini. When the page finally opened, her maths score sat in red. She had failed the advanced paper she'd switched to in July. Chetan, dripping under the tin roof, shook his head. "Honestly, it was obvious. Anyone could see the advanced paper was a trap." Yamini stared at him. "Two weeks ago you said it was a smart move. You said you'd pick it too." "That was different," Chetan said, then stopped, because he couldn't explain how. The screen flickered off again. In the dark, Yamini picked up her umbrella and walked out into the rain without waiting for the lights. Chetan stayed by the dead monitor, still sure he had seen it coming, and not sure why she was so upset.

qa.q: Why did the results take so long to load for Yamini?
qa.a: Rain had flooded the lane and the power kept dipping, so the mock-test results took ten minutes to load.

qa.q: Why does Chetan feel so sure the result was obvious?
qa.a: Now that he knows the score, the risk looks clear, so he feels confident and a little superior, as if he had seen it coming; he forgets he called the switch a smart move two weeks earlier.

qa.q: What could Chetan try before judging a choice after the results are out?
qa.a: He could ask himself what he honestly thought before the results, remember that he had praised the advanced paper, and comfort Yamini instead of judging her.

qa.q: How does Yamini see Chetan's comment?
qa.a: To Yamini it feels unfair and hurtful, because he backed her choice before and now blames her only because of how it turned out 😔

grounding: Shows a teenager calling a failed exam choice obvious once the result is known, although he had thought it was a smart choice beforehand.

passage:
Monday: Salma sat at the back of the film club meeting, taking minutes. Elizabeth suggested the open lawn for Saturday's screening. The forecast showed a slight chance of drizzle, the hall cost extra, and every hand went up.
Saturday: A sudden gust tore the screen off its frame twenty minutes into the film. Salma helped stack wet chairs while Elizabeth apologised to each guest at the gate.
Wednesday: At the review, Dhruv leaned back. "Honestly, the lawn was an obvious risk. Elizabeth should have seen it coming." Two others nodded. Elizabeth stared at the table. Salma opened her notebook and read Monday's minutes aloud: the forecast, the hall price, the vote. "So what did we actually know on Monday?" she asked. The room went quiet. Then someone said, "Maybe a backup plan for wind, next time." Elizabeth finally looked up.

qa.q: What did the forecast show on Monday?
qa.a: The forecast showed a slight chance of drizzle.

qa.q: What might Salma be feeling when the others nod along with Dhruv?
qa.a: She is likely uneasy and protective of Elizabeth, because her own minutes show that everyone voted for the lawn with what they knew on Monday.

qa.q: Which step made the review fairer, and why?
qa.a: Reading Monday's minutes and asking what was known then, because it separated the decision from the bad luck of the gust and turned blame into a backup plan.

qa.q: What is it like for Elizabeth when Dhruv calls the risk obvious?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels singled out and ashamed, even though the whole club voted for the lawn.

grounding: Shows a club review calling a failed event's risk obvious, and an observer asking what was actually known when the choice was made.

passage: Sabina, sit, the chai is still hot. You look the way I looked after my first bad review. When I was twenty-five, I ran the dispatch desk at a small garment unit in Tiruppur. One monsoon a shipment went out late, and the owner wanted a name. Imran had suggested the slower route, but I had agreed to it, and I watched him wait to be blamed. After that, before every big call, I wrote in a notebook: what we expected, why, and how sure we felt. Months later another order slipped. We opened the notebook together. The reasons had been sound; a lorry strike was plain bad luck. Imran kept his job and began writing down his own guesses. People laughed and called me "Hansa the notebook." Let them laugh, I thought. Fewer people cried in our reviews after that.

qa.q: What did Hansa write in the notebook before every big call?
qa.a: Hansa wrote what they expected, why, and how sure they felt.

qa.q: What was young Hansa worried about after the first late shipment?
qa.a: Hansa felt uneasy and guilty, because Imran was waiting to be blamed for a route Hansa had also agreed to.

qa.q: Which choice in the story changed how later reviews went, and why?
qa.a: Writing down expectations and reasons before each big call, because when the next order slipped, the team could see the decision was sound and the lorry strike was bad luck.

qa.q: How might Imran see the notebook after the second delay?
qa.a: For Imran it became a relief and a protection, since it showed his reasoning had been sound, so he started writing down his own guesses.

grounding: Illustrates a lead who records forecasts and reasons before outcomes, so later reviews separate the decision from luck and fewer people are blamed.

passage: The colony's Diwali fair smelled of smoke and sugar. Madhav had begged for the tall paper cone of spicy chana, and Jagdish uncle at the stall had charged thirty rupees for it. Three bites in, his tongue burned and his eyes watered. He hated it. Still, he kept eating, one slow chickpea at a time, while sparklers fizzed near the gate. "Throw it, beta, you're crying," said his mother. "No! It cost thirty rupees," Madhav said, fanning his mouth. "If I throw it, the money is gone." He finished the whole cone on the steps with a red face and a steel tumbler of water, and missed the rangoli prize being announced.

qa.q: How much did the spicy chana cost?
qa.a: It cost thirty rupees.

qa.q: Why does Madhav keep eating the chana even though his tongue burns?
qa.a: He feels worried and a bit guilty that throwing it away would waste the thirty rupees, so finishing it feels like the careful, sensible thing to do.

qa.q: What could Madhav's mother say to help him next time?
qa.a: She could gently explain that the thirty rupees are spent whether he eats it or not, so he can stop and still enjoy the fair.

qa.q: How might Madhav's mother feel watching him finish the cone?
qa.a: She is probably worried and a little exasperated, seeing him suffer and miss the rangoli prize over money that was already spent.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps eating food he dislikes because it was paid for, treating past spending as a reason to continue.

subtype: Stuck in coaching or a course [Actor]
passage:
Holi colours were still pink on Kunal's elbows when he dropped his coaching bag by the door.
"You're back early," Pooja didi said, scrubbing green off her own cheeks.
"Class got cut short. Didi, I hate chemistry. I sit there and nothing goes in."
"So stop. You want to do design anyway."
"Stop? Papa has paid two years of fees. Two years, didi. If I stop now, all that is just wasted."
"It's already paid. It won't come back if you suffer through one more year."
"But then it was all for nothing." He rubbed at the colour on his arm. "And what do I tell Papa?"
"Tell him you want your evenings for the sketches you keep drawing at midnight."
"He'll say I gave up."
"Or he'll say you finally chose something." She tossed him the soap. "Wash first. Then we talk to him together."

qa.q: How many years of fees has Papa paid for Kunal's coaching?
qa.a: Papa has paid two years of fees.

qa.q: What is Kunal afraid of when he thinks about stopping?
qa.a: He is afraid the two years will feel wasted and that Papa will think he gave up, so staying feels safer even though he hates chemistry.

qa.q: What small step could Kunal take next?
qa.a: He could sit down with Papa and Pooja, talk honestly about wanting his evenings for design, and judge the choice from today forward instead of by the fees already paid.

qa.q: How does Pooja see Kunal's worry about the fees?
qa.a: Pooja sees that the money is already gone, and that another unhappy year would only cost Kunal time he could give to his sketches.

grounding: Shows a teenager staying in a coaching class he hates because of the fees and years already spent, at the cost of time for what he wants.

passage: During the Sankranti break, the fields around Kondapur were stubble and kite string. Raghav spent the whole morning under the old water pump behind the temple, and by noon it was running again. Anjali, who studied at the same town college, watched him wipe grease off his hands. "You look happier now than in two years of accounts class," she said. "I'm leaving B.Com after this semester. I've got a seat in the ITI electrical course." Raghav laughed too loudly. "And throw away two years? Amma sold her gold earrings for my first fee." "Those years are spent either way." He looked at the humming pump, then down the road to the bus stand where the college bus would leave on Monday. "If I leave now, it means everything was a waste," he said, and walked home to find his ledger notebooks.

qa.q: What did Raghav repair during the Sankranti break?
qa.a: He repaired the old water pump behind the temple.

qa.q: Why does leaving B.Com feel so hard for Raghav?
qa.a: He feels guilty and scared that leaving would make the two years, and Amma's gold earrings, feel wasted, so staying seems like the loyal choice.

qa.q: What question could help Raghav decide more fairly?
qa.a: He could ask which course he would choose if he were starting today, knowing how much he enjoys repair work, and talk it through with Amma and a college counsellor.

qa.q: How does Anjali see Raghav's choice?
qa.a: Anjali sees that he is happiest working on the pump and believes the spent years should not decide his future, just as they did not decide hers.

grounding: Shows a student staying in a degree that no longer fits because leaving would make the earlier years and a family sacrifice feel wasted.

passage:
Onam night
Everyone is asleep after the sadya, and I'm on the back steps with the last of the payasam.
Achan brought up the exam again at lunch. "We have already paid for the coaching, the test, the counsellor. The whole family knows you are going abroad." I smiled and passed the avial.
The truth: I like my job at the bank branch. I don't want to leave for two years and start over.
Called Kavitha at ten. She said, "Ganga, their money is spent whatever you choose. What they want is for you to be settled. Tell them kindly, before the application deadline."
So I wrote down what I'll say: thank you first, for all of it. Then the truth, gently. After breakfast tomorrow, before I lose my nerve. 😔

qa.q: What does Achan say the family has already paid for?
qa.a: The coaching, the test and the counsellor.

qa.q: Why did Ganga smile and pass the avial instead of answering Achan?
qa.a: Ganga felt pressured and guilty, because the family's money and pride were already tied to the plan, so speaking up felt like letting them down.

qa.q: What would you advise Ganga for tomorrow's talk?
qa.a: Begin with thanks, then say honestly and kindly what Ganga wants, and invite Achan to talk about the choice from here on, not about what was already spent.

qa.q: How might Achan feel when Ganga tells the truth?
qa.a: Achan may feel disappointed at first because the family expected this plan, but also relieved to finally know what Ganga really wants.

grounding: Shows a young worker pressured to continue a costly plan because of the parents' spent money and pride, and preparing a kind, honest conversation.

passage: Last March I sat in the lab in Aizawl with two years of fish samples in the freezer and a thesis going nowhere. My supervisor had moved to another university, the stream had changed course after the floods, and every new sample made the data messier. Lavanya, who shared my bench, found me staring at the freezer. "Go home, Lalremsiami," she said. I didn't. I asked myself the question an old teacher once gave me: if I were choosing a topic today, knowing all this, would I pick this one? I wanted to say yes. I couldn't. That night I cried properly, for the fieldwork, the muddy boots, the dawn buses. Then I wrote one page on what those years taught me: careful sampling, patience, asking for help sooner. In April I began a smaller project on the new stream bed. I'm not ashamed of that freezer anymore.

qa.q: What had happened to the stream?
qa.a: The stream had changed course after the floods.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami feel that night, and why?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt deep grief for the fieldwork, the muddy boots and the dawn buses, because the honest answer meant letting two years of work go 🤍

qa.q: Which step helped Lalremsiami move on without shame?
qa.a: Writing one page on what the two years taught, then starting a smaller project, so the lost time became learning instead of a reason to keep going.

qa.q: How might Lavanya be affected by Lalremsiami's decision?
qa.a: Lavanya is likely relieved to see Lalremsiami stop staring at the freezer and start fresh work that feels lighter.

grounding: Shows a person asking whether they would start the project today knowing what they know now, then grieving the cost, learning from it and moving on without shame.

passage: Fog hung over the colony park in Ludhiana so thickly that the swings looked grey. Hemant and Gurpreet crouched beside a circle scratched in the cold dirt, fingers stiff inside their woollen gloves. Hemant's first shot knocked one of Gurpreet's marbles out of the ring. He pocketed it with a small "yes" and moved on. Two turns later Gurpreet hit Hemant's blue-swirl marble clean out of the circle. Hemant's face crumpled. He sat back on his heels and wailed, loud enough that a man walking his dog turned around. "It's just one," said Gurpreet. "You won one of mine." "It's not the same!" Hemant sobbed, staring at his empty palm while the fog swallowed the far end of the park.

qa.q: What happened on Hemant's first shot?
qa.a: Hemant's first shot knocked one of Gurpreet's marbles out of the ring.

qa.q: Why does losing the blue-swirl marble upset Hemant so much more than winning one pleased him?
qa.a: The blue-swirl marble was already his, so losing it feels like something taken away; he feels hurt and cheated, while the won marble only felt like a small extra.

qa.q: How could an adult help Hemant calm down?
qa.a: They could let him be sad for a moment, then point out that he won one and lost one, so he has the same number of marbles as when he started.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet see Hemant's crying?
qa.a: Gurpreet is puzzled, because to Gurpreet the game is even: Hemant won one marble and lost one.

grounding: Shows a child crying harder over losing a marble than he celebrated winning an equal one.

subtype: Fear of losing rank or friends [Actor]
passage:
Monday, first week of the monsoon term: Trisha stopped Naveen outside the lab. "Basketball trials on Thursday. You're tall, just come." Naveen said he'd think about it. He was the chess club's best player, and everyone there asked him for advice.
Thursday: Rain drummed on the roof of the covered court. Naveen stood in the doorway with his chess bag, watching kids miss easy shots and laugh about it. He pictured himself missing too, in front of all of them, and turned towards the chess room instead. He won three games. None of them felt like much.
Three weeks later: The basketball group had its own jokes now, and Trisha sat with them at lunch. Naveen ate with the chess club as usual, glancing across the canteen more often than he meant to.

qa.q: Where did Naveen go on Thursday instead of the trials?
qa.a: He turned towards the chess room instead and won three games.

qa.q: What was Naveen worried about at the court doorway?
qa.a: He was anxious about missing shots in front of everyone and losing the respect he had as the chess club's best player, so walking away felt safer 😰

qa.q: What small step could Naveen have tried?
qa.a: He could have tried the trials just once while keeping chess, treating a few missed shots as the normal cost of learning something new.

qa.q: How might Trisha see Naveen after the trials?
qa.a: Trisha may feel a little let down that Naveen never came, and may stop inviting him, which leaves him watching the basketball group from across the canteen.

grounding: Shows a teenager avoiding a new sport and group because losing his current standing feels worse than any gain, so his world stays small.
